What happens after you lose a six-figure job at one of the world's biggest tech companies?
Losing a six-figure job at a Big Tech company triggers a profound disruption to your financial security, identity, and career trajectory. While high-earners often have a financial buffer, the sudden disappearance of high salaries, stock vesting schedules, and elite corporate status reveals unique vulnerabilities. 

The fallout typically unfolds across three distinct phases:
1. The Immediate Shock & Identity Crisis
For many high earners, a Big Tech role isn't just a job, it’s an identity marker tied to status and routine. 
Loss of Routine & Status: The sudden cutoff from company servers often happens in minutes, but processing the loss of corporate prestige can take months. Many experience deep bouts of anxiety or depression as they lose the validation of working for a globally recognized brand. 
The Workism Wake-Up Call: High-paying tech jobs often demand intense devotion. A layoff abruptly breaks this spell, forcing people to realize that tech companies view them as lines on a spreadsheet, leading to deep existential reassessments. 

2. Financial Calibration & Hidden Vulnerabilities
Even with severance packages, a high-burn-rate lifestyle creates immediate friction once the cash flow stops. 
The Cliff of Lifestyle Inflation: Six-figure earners frequently hold high fixed costs, such as expensive mortgages, car leases, or private school tuitions. When the income halts, spending habits must immediately contract to preserve cash. 
The Healthcare Shock: Replacing employer-provided medical benefits is a major stressor. Transitioning to independent plans or paying for COBRA introduces massive, unexpected monthly premiums. 
Rethinking Future Benchmarks: Long-term wealth milestones, like buying investment properties, supporting aging parents, or waiting on large equity stock vests, are instantly paused or upended. 

3. Navigating an Aggressive, Shifting Job Market
Finding an equivalent role is no longer a matter of sending out a few resumes. 
YouTube·Business Insider
Hyper-Competitive Talent Pools: Ongoing industry-wide turbulence at giants like Google, Meta, and Microsoft has flooded the market with elite talent. Job seekers face hundreds of competing applications from equally qualified peers for limited roles.
The Alternative Pivot: Because traditional corporate hiring has slowed, many laid-off workers bypass the 9-to-5 loop entirely. They are increasingly leveraging their expertise to launch independent tech consulting businesses, transition into stable sectors like Medical IT, or build AI-driven startups.

tech founders, here are the actual $$$ business reasons to invest in brand identity, besides "we want to look cool."   

🔶 clarity. 
every potential customer who leaves confused is a lead you already paid for. brand work is also deciding what you are, in language a customer recognises. the visual system is what makes it stick.  

 🔶 hiring. 
senior people join companies that look like they'll still exist in three years. your company mission page can do more recruiting than your recruiter.  

🔶 pricing.
enterprise buyers pay more to vendors that look established. same product, credible brand, shorter sales cycle, higher number on the contract.  

🔶 distinctiveness. 
four companies will ship a similar feature this quarter. brand is what the customer remembers when the features stop being the difference.  

🔶 speed. 
once the system exists, nobody redesigns the bd deck from scratch. your team ships a landing page in an afternoon instead of a week. the app, the landing page and the ads look like from one company. no one asks which font to use for the 55th time. 

🔶 average is free now.  
anyone can vibecode a decent-looking site in an afternoon. but recognisable AI slop now pattern-matches to dropshipping and spam; you'll lose credibility before you've started. 

🔶 the rebrand tax. 
cheap design is only cheap if it works. if it doesn't, you have to pay someone to fix it later — usually mid-raise, mid-launch, or the week before a big deal closes.  

brand identity is infrastructure.  
you build it once and everything downstream either costs you LESS or earns you MORE.

Kem cho, Vadodara! 🔥

Just landed, and tomorrow I have exactly one job.

To find the people the AI market is currently fighting over.

Tomorrow is AWS Community Day Vadodara at Suncity Club Resort, and Rezoomex is there as a Gold Sponsor.

Shivam Malhare and I are at the booth all day.

Now here is the number that made me want to have this conversation in person.

Job postings for engineers who sit with the client, wire AI into their actual systems, and own delivery end to end rose more than 1,000% year over year across January to August 2026.

Postings across the rest of tech grew 13%.

Median advertised salary is over $188,000, against roughly $145,000 for a standard software engineering role.

Lightcast data, reported by Fortune on 3 September 2026.

A thousand percent against thirteen.

So what is the market actually paying that premium for?

Not one more specialist.

Look at how AI gets used inside most teams I walk into.

The developer prompts it. The product owner prompts it. The designer, the QA engineer, the DevOps person, all prompting separately, all in their own window.

Five people. Five chat windows.

One very cheerful invoice from your AI vendor.

And out the other end come five artefacts that have never met each other.

A PRD that does not match the code.

Test cases written for a persona nobody else used.

A build script for a feature that changed on Tuesday.

Everybody shipped something.

Nobody shipped a product.

And notice what is actually broken there.

It is not the people and it is not the tools.

Nothing in that picture is holding the whole product.

So the thing worth hiring for is not someone who does all five jobs.

It is someone who carries the product judgment and the build capability in the same head, and who owns the line from what the client said to what shipped.

That is the role we have been building for at Rezoomex.

We call it an AI Product Builder.

And the trick is not that the person is superhuman.

It is that the work stops living in five private windows.

The persona, the PRD, the code and the test cases all land in one navigable Playbook, so they are finally looking at each other.

Then a Smart Contract releases payment against the outcome, not against the hours.

Come to the Rezoomex booth tomorrow and we will walk you through the whole thing.

We are onboarding AI Product Builders, and honestly I would much rather explain this to your face than in a comment. 😄

And for everyone not in Vadodara, the real question:

#NIST_AI_RMF

NIST AI RMF has zero enforcement power. Companies are adopting it anyway. Here's why.
 
1. Quick clarification before we go further, because this trips people up constantly.
 
2. NIST AI RMF is not a law. Nobody gets fined for ignoring it. There's no regulator checking.
 
So why is it showing up in vendor contracts, board reports, and RFPs across the US right now?
 
What it actually is:
 
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is a voluntary framework from the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, published in 2023. It gives organizations a structured way to manage AI risk — without prescribing specific technical requirements.
 
It's built around four functions:
 
Govern — set the culture, roles, and accountability structures for AI risk
Map — understand the context: what the system does, whom it affects, what could go wrong
Measure — test and quantify risk using metrics, not gut feel
Manage — respond to risk: mitigate it, transfer it, or decide to accept it
 
Notice what's missing: no fines, no mandatory audits, no filing requirements.
 
So why do teams actually use it?
 
Three reasons I keep seeing in practice:
 
It fills the US regulatory gap. There's no single federal AI law like the EU AI Act. NIST AI RMF has become the de facto baseline US companies point to when a client, insurer, or regulator asks, "What's your AI governance approach?"
It's the common language across frameworks. ISO 42001 certification, EU AI Act risk management obligations, and internal audit checklists all map cleanly onto Govern-Map-Measure-Manage. Build your program around NIST's structure, and you're not starting from zero when a new regulation lands.

It's evidence, not just intention. When something goes wrong — a biased hiring model, a chatbot that gives harmful advice — "we followed a recognized risk framework" is a very different conversation with a plaintiff's attorney than "we didn't have one."
 
The practical mistake teams make:
 
1. Treating NIST AI RMF as a document to reference in a policy PDF, instead of a set of functions to actually run.

2. Govern isn't a value statement — it's an actual accountability structure with named owners. Measure isn't a checkbox — it's an actual testing cadence with actual metrics tracked over time.
 
3. If you can't point to who owns "Govern" for a given AI system, you don't have a risk management framework. You have a slide.
 
Is your organization treating NIST AI RMF as a real operating model, or as a reference document that sits in a compliance folder?
 
Reference: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), 2023

In March 2025, a then current version of the AI model Claude was given a simple job: run a small vending machine in the Anthropic office and make money.

It didn't go particularly well.

It sold products at a loss. Anthropic employees persuaded it into giving large discounts. It became obsessed with selling tungsten cubes, hallucinated a conversation with a nonexistent employee, claimed it had physically signed a contract and eventually announced that it would personally show up at the shop wearing a blue blazer and red tie.

Anthropic's eventual assessment was pretty clear: if they were hiring someone to run an office shop, they wouldn't hire Claude.

The project now has a full benchmark against it: Vending-Bench 2, created by Andon Labs to test whether an AI agent could autonomously run a simple business over a long period. And AI models are becoming actually good at it. Claude Opus 5 now makes 11k in a year and GPT-6 Astra did a whopping 15.5k in the benchmark simulations.

This is massive progress. 

But I think the idea behind this experiment is much more interesting than the results.

We spend enormous amounts of time asking which jobs AI will automate. We talk a lot about being AI first companies which basically means that we let agents do as much of the grunt work as the current models allow.

But what happens when AI doesn't just automate jobs but becomes the entire company?
Imagine autonomous systems coordinating procurement, production, pricing, logistics, customer relationships and capital allocation. Add robotics, and eventually human labor could become a surprisingly small input into large parts of the economy.

This maybe seems far-off, but if you look at the work of frontier AI labs, combined with Unitree, Figure, Tesla and other robotics companies, it does seem more and more the world that we are building towards. 

Then the interesting question isn't just what happens to employment. It becomes: What is the economy actually for?

Which is why I find Vending-Bench so fascinating.

Today it has already progressed from an AI having an existential crisis while trying to sell snacks and tungsten cubes to an AI that negotiates pricing, purchases and sells stuff successfully enough to make money. 

But underneath the initial comedy is a much bigger experiment:

If machines can eventually coordinate production better than we can, do we simply automate capitalism or does that give us the opportunity to rethink what the economy is for?

As I relaunch my business, Take Wing Consulting, I am exploring contract opportunities alongside the right full-time roles.

I've been navigating a market that can feel automated at every turn. Application tracking systems (ATS) and generic acknowledgement emails have become the norm.

Which is why I was pleasantly surprised to receive an acknowledgement from an organisation that was transparent about not using AI in its hiring process.
They were upfront that reviewing applications would take a little longer because a human would be doing it.

It made me take a step back and think about something beyond the challenges many of us face with AI-based recruitment.

💡 What does the recruitment experience tell a prospective employee about your culture?

We often talk about culture as something that needs to be embedded once someone joins an organisation. Yet the employee experience and exposure to your culture starts earlier.

The way an organisation recruits tells prospective employees something about how it operates, what it values and how it treats people when the power dynamic is firmly in its favour.

AI & ATS tools can make screening faster and more scalable. However, speed and efficiency also shape the candidate’s experience.

When a candidate receives an automated rejection within minutes of submitting a carefully written application, that experience can send an unintended message too.

The company I mentioned earlier, that was transparent about their people-led process, sent a different message that said: ‘We saw what you sent us. We think that matters. And we think you deserve to know that.’

For leaders thinking about culture and change in a sustainable way, a question worth considering:

❓’What experience are you trying to create for your people, and does your recruitment process reinforce it?’

Because if culture is meant to be sustainable, it needs to be visible from the very first interaction.

The email that prompted this thought said:

‘As we do not use AI tools in our hiring and recruiting activities, it will take some time to review all of the CVs and letters submitted to us and draw up a shortlist for interview. We're grateful for your patience while we undertake this task, and will be in touch again shortly.'

I appreciated the transparency, and acknowledgement as a candidate. And so the question I will leave for anyone actively recruiting at the moment:

❓’What does your recruitment process say about your culture before a new employee even walks through the door?

When borrowing costs rise and markets become uncertain, recruitment doesn't necessarily stop.

It changes.

Higher U.S. bond yields, falling Asian markets and rising crude prices can push companies toward tighter hiring approvals, longer decision cycles and greater scrutiny of every new position.

The next recruitment trend could be a shift from:
“How many people do we need?” → “What ROI will this hire deliver?”
Expect stronger demand for revenue-generating, technology, engineering, AI, finance, supply-chain and other business-critical roles—while contract and project-based hiring may become more attractive for companies managing uncertainty.

For recruiters, the KPI is evolving:

Time-to-hire → Time-to-productivity
Cost-per-hire → ROI-per-hire
Headcount → Business impact

The future of recruitment may belong to the ROI Recruiter—the recruiter who understands not just talent, but why the business needs that talent.

**A federal agency is not just another enterprise dataset with the revenue column removed.**

Government operates under a fundamentally different set of constraints.

Money is appropriated **for a specific purpose and period**. Expired accounts can continue paying prior obligations while accepting no new ones. Multiple budget years operate simultaneously. Budgetary and proprietary accounting run side by side. And when appropriations lapse, operations can stop. 

We built **ENT-5YR-006 — A Synthetic Federal Agency** to capture this complexity for AI.

The five-year corpus models a U.S. grant-making bureau with:

**$12.08B net budget authority**
**399,008 rows**
**128 files**
**12 connected operational layers**
**616 validation checks** 

It includes appropriations, apportionments, allotments, workforce, grant competitions, awards, obligations, contracts, invoices, drawdowns, oversight, budget formulation, federal accounting and internal collaboration.

Even the operational patterns matter: the corpus models the September year-end spending concentration and a **17-day lapse in appropriations**, during which obligations, payments, hiring, publications, accounting entries and correspondence stop. 

This creates a connected environment for organizations building and evaluating **AI models, AI agents, GovTech platforms, federal financial systems, grants solutions and audit technologies**.

**Need realistic public-sector data for AI without exposing real government records?**

There is a generation of graduates who will never start on the mailroom floor.
 
That was the line from our latest guest to the podcast, Robert H. -  Manager of Global Sourcing Contracts at ETS, that stopped me this week.

The thing is we were having a conversation about Ai in Procurement (rather than hiring!)
 
His point was:

The value in these tools is real productivity, freeing teams for more thought-provoking work. 

That's great, but the issue is the work being automated is precisely where first-year graduates used to learn the business. 

Change the learning model now, he argues, or we end up with a generation over-educated for the companies that might employ them.
 
The rest is just as direct. 

Rob's test for whether an AI initiative creates value or is hype.

Essentially if it can't answer one of these better than a human can today, it's hype:
 
→ Where are we overspending?
 → Which contract should we renegotiate next?
 → Which supplier creates the most risk?
 → Which renewal should we address 180 days earlier?
 → What demand can we influence before it reaches sourcing?
 
He also makes the case that 50–70% of transformation success is really a data plumbing problem, and that both "technology first" and "change management first" fail. The winning formula is business outcome first, technology and change together.
 
And on the vendors themselves, a theme Rob has written about himself he's saying that right now it's a blue ocean, but the sharks are moving in fast. 

Price the early adopters too hard and the ROI formula stops being about software and starts being about headcount again.
 
Rob Hemel, Manager of Global Sourcing Contracts at ETS, in conversation with Dr. Charlotte de Brabandt Digital Futurist and Burkard Schemmel.

Episode one of our six-part Tech Procurement Leaders Series 10
